hints: Count the peptide bonds in the diagram and look at the side chain (R group) on each alpha carbon. There are three residues, so hydrolysis must give three separate amino acids.

Hydrolysis breaks each -CO-NH- peptide bond and restores -COOH and -NH2, but the R groups stay exactly the same. Compare the R groups CH2CONH2, CH2OH and CH3 in the peptide with the R groups in options A to D.
walkthrough:
**Spot the tripeptide and its peptide bonds**

Look along the backbone from left to right. You can see two -CO-NH- peptide bonds joining three amino acid residues.

Complete hydrolysis means adding water across each peptide bond to break it, so we will get three free amino acids, each with the general form $H_2N-CH(R)-COOH$.

**Read off the three R groups**

Focus only on the group attached to each central alpha carbon.

Left residue: $R = CH_2-C(=O)-NH_2$. This is asparagine.
Middle residue: $R = CH_2-OH$. This is serine.
Right residue: $R = CH_3$. This is alanine.

Remember, hydrolysis does not change R groups.

**Match to the options**

We need one asparagine plus one serine plus one alanine, all shown as free amino acids with $-NH_2$ and $-COOH$.

Only option C shows exactly $H_2N-CH(CH_2CONH_2)-COOH$, $H_2N-CH(CH_2OH)-COOH$ and $H_2N-CH(CH_3)-COOH$. That is the correct set.

options.A: Incorrect. The middle (serine) and right (alanine) are correct, but the left amino acid has R = CH2CH2CONH2 instead of CH2CONH2. That extra CH2 is wrong.
options.B: Incorrect. The left (asparagine) and right (alanine) are correct, but the middle amino acid has R = CH(OH)CH3 instead of CH2OH. That is a different amino acid.
options.C: Correct. It shows asparagine with R = CH2CONH2, serine with R = CH2OH, and alanine with R = CH3, exactly the three residues from hydrolysis.
options.D: Incorrect. The left (asparagine) and middle (serine) are correct, but the right amino acid has R = H instead of CH3. That would be glycine, not alanine.
